help.toolbox: Your instruments. Choose one and it casts its sight where you face; R re-casts it from wherever you stand. The dots are how firmly each is held — a firmer hold reads narrower.
help.readout: The chosen instrument's reading, standing in the world. Set the release angle below (type an exact number if you already know it), then throw with Space.
help.gate: A counting gate. The carved rule asks for a count: type it and set it. The beam tips toward the heavier side by exactly the difference — brought level, it lifts and the way opens.
help.door: The door takes two numbers — the two where the lintel's rule comes to rest. Set both slots; the frame only lets go for the right pair, in any order.
help.stone: A way into the practice-yard. Enter, train, and return to the spot you left.
help.doc: The level's end, for now. Everything you did on the way is in the log.
help.log: Everything this session did, timestamped, newest first. Download keeps it as a file.
help.cold-well: A counterweighted hoist. Jars sit on the sunken tray; iron rings hang opposite, some already fixed. Count both, type how many rings to add, and the crank does the rest — balance rises steadily; a wrong count runs away at the speed of its error.
help.lamp-road: Each lamp turns cups of oil into a fixed count of light-flags toward the next post. Count the dark flags and pour exactly enough. Too little leaves the remainder dark to count again; too much carries on and lights the start of the next stretch.
help.gathering-frames: The press tray takes one fig per hollow, no more. Count the basket against the tray, set aside the difference, then tip. Misjudge it and the extra bruises on the grass — or the beam refuses a tray with empty hollows.
help.mill-launder: Six collars set the channel's fall, and the headstone carves the rule they must follow. E at a post sets its collar; the sluice sends the water as far as the rule holds — it spills exactly where the rule breaks.
help.bell-yard: Hang the bell on the knot where the falling path will cross the cord, then watch the spark ride the rule — it rings only the truth. Five hangs make your measure, and the yard grades how firmly the Falling Arc is held. The return stone takes you back.

architect.concept: trajectory unit: diagnostic fork, misconception branches, physical rejoin, two good ways converging

instruments.name: Counting Cord
instruments.blurb: A knotted cord. It counts paces and nothing else.

architect.note: A genuinely inapplicable option. Choosing it is not punished — it reads a distance.

instruments.name: Plumb & Level
instruments.blurb: Sights a straight line from your hand. It has no notion of falling.

architect.note: Law 3 — the straight line is the honest first-order reading, and the player watches it be wrong.

instruments.name: The Falling Arc
instruments.blurb: Reads the whole path of a thrown thing, and where it passes a given height.

architect.note: Held at partial strength on purpose. Law 5 — the arc reads as a band and the crossings as ranges, never a confident wrong number.

hintLadder.text: You are carrying three instruments. One of them reads paths.
A thrown stone does not travel in a straight line. Whatever you sight with must know that.
The Falling Arc is the instrument for this.
Cast the sight at the fig, then set the release so a crossing of the fig's height lands on it.
